topics: 🧰 'Sustain Him' — the verse behind leaving a debtor food, clothing, and his craft's tools
📿 A Sold Man's Tefillin — Rav Yeimar's ruling that even an ordinary sale includes them
👕 What Can Never Be Taken — a wife's garments, dyed clothes, new sandals, and the 'here and now' rule
🌾 Consecrating an Ancestral Field Near the Jubilee — the two-year and one-year fences
🎉 Consecrating a Field DURING the Jubilee Itself — Rav vs. Shmuel on whether it takes effect at all

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Protected Possessions and the Jubilee Field
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 24a–24b
overview.hebrewSource: וְאִם מָךְ הוּא מֵעֶרְכֶּךָ — הַחֲיֵיהוּ מֵעֶרְכֶּךָ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes explaining why a debtor keeps food, clothing, and trade tools even as the Temple treasury repossesses his other property, then turns to what even a person who consecrates literally everything must still give up (his tefillin) and what may never be seized from anyone — his family's clothing and anything not yet worth its later, appreciated price. With that, the chapter on proclaiming sales closes. A new mishna opens a fresh topic: the special two-year and one-year windows around the Jubilee Year that govern when an ancestral field may be consecrated or redeemed, and a sharp Rav-and-Shmuel dispute over what happens if someone consecrates his field during the Jubilee Year itself.

slides.title: 🧰 Why the Debtor Keeps His Tools
slides.subtitle: Scripture, and a very practical worry, behind the mishna's leniency

steps.content: 1️⃣ Source verse: 'if he be too poor for your valuation' (Lev. 27:8) is read as הַחֲיֵיהוּ מֵעֶרְכֶּךָ — 'sustain him' out of his own valuation debt
2️⃣ 'Him' — but explicitly not his wife or children, who are not mentioned in the verse
3️⃣ If he had many of one tool and few of another (e.g. three adzes, one saw), the treasury does not sell the extras to buy him a matching pair
4️⃣ Why is this not obvious, since one saw always sufficed before? Because until now he could borrow a second tool if needed — now, newly poor, no one will lend to him

slides.title: 📿 Even Tefillin Are Not Safe From a Full Consecration
slides.subtitle: A real case brought before Rav Yeimar
slides.label: The incident:
slides.text: A man had sold all his property. When the case came before Rav Yeimar, he ruled: remove even his tefillin and give them to the buyer. This might seem obvious from the mishna's own rule that consecrating all one's property includes the tefillin — but the Gemara explains the case teaches something new: perhaps one might think tefillin are excluded only from a straightforward sale (since a person would not silently sell an item used for a mitzva performed with his own body without saying so explicitly) even while they're included in a mitzva-driven consecration. Rav Yeimar's ruling shows tefillin are swept into an unqualified sale of 'everything' just as they are into an unqualified consecration.
slides.hebrewSource: הַמַּקְדִּישׁ אֶת נְכָסָיו מַעֲלִין לוֹ תְּפִילִּין

slides.title: 👕 What the Temple Treasury May Never Touch
slides.subtitle: New mishna: absolute protections, plus a 'here and now' valuation rule
rows: Both one who consecrates property and one who valuates himself
Never part of his own liened property
Dyed garments made for them, even unworn
Intent to give already removes them from his estate
Full future/appreciated value (fine garments on a slave, a cow held for market day, a pearl brought to the city)
'Give your valuation on that day' (Lev. 27:23) — no delaying a sale to chase a higher price elsewhere

callout.label: Bonus teaching:
callout.text: The same verse's phrase 'holy to the Lord' teaches that unspecified consecrations (simply 'my property is consecrated') go to Temple maintenance (bedek habayit), not to the priests.

slides.title: 🌾 New Mishna: Fencing Off the Jubilee Year
slides.subtitle: Why 'less than two years before' and 'less than one year after' the Jubilee are off-limits

nodes.content: ❓ Mishna: one may not consecrate an ancestral field less than 2 years before the Jubilee, nor redeem one less than 1 year after it. But a baraita says fields may be consecrated any time except during the Jubilee Year itself — contradiction?
💡 Rav and Shmuel together: the mishna's '2 years' bars only redemption with a deduction (gerua, prorated by years left) — not consecration itself, which always remains valid

✅ Practical effect: consecrate less than 2 years out, and you (or your heirs) simply pay the full 50-sela valuation rather than a discounted, year-prorated sum — 'let a person be concerned for his property'

slides.title: 🎉 Consecrating a Field DURING the Jubilee Year Itself
slides.subtitle: Rav and Shmuel read the same verse two different ways

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: It is consecrated — and one redeems it for the full fifty sela per beit kor. The verse 'if he sanctifies his field from the Jubilee Year' (Lev. 27:17) includes the Jubilee Year itself in that opening word.

lines.speaker: Shmuel
lines.text: It is not consecrated at all! 'From the Jubilee Year' means starting the year after — the Jubilee Year itself is excluded.

lines.speaker: Rav Yosef's challenge
lines.text: For a sale, Shmuel's logic makes sense by an a fortiori: even an already-sold field reverts at the Jubilee, so an unsold one surely can't be newly sold then. But for consecration, doesn't a parallel mishna show a field consecrated earlier does NOT simply revert at the Jubilee — the priests receive its value?

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds the priests enter the field without any payment — so the a fortiori does hold after all. Rav disputes even this, since the field still leaves hekdesh (to priests, 'from the Table of the Most High'), not back to the original owner.

summary.principle: The Torah protects a debtor's basic livelihood — food, clothing, trade tools, and his family's belongings — even while collecting valuations, though total consecration takes everything including tefillin; and an ancestral field's consecration near the Jubilee Year follows its own precise, disputed timing rules.

flowSteps.content: 🧰 'Sustain him' (Lev. 27:8) protects the debtor's food, clothes, bed, and trade tools — but never his family's
📿 Rav Yeimar: even an ordinary sale of 'everything' sweeps in tefillin, just like full consecration does

columns.content: 👕 A wife's/children's clothing is always protected; valuation is fixed to 'that day,' not future appreciated value
🌾 The 2-year/1-year Jubilee fences limit redemption-with-deduction, not consecration itself

flowSteps.content: 🎉 Rav: a field consecrated during the Jubilee itself is valid, full price; Shmuel: it never takes effect at all
🎓 Key Principle: precise verses ('sustain him,' 'from the Jubilee Year,' 'on that day') calibrate exactly how far Temple collection may reach into a person's life and property

quiz.q: Why does the mishna's list of protected items (food, clothing, bed, tools) apply only to the debtor himself and not to his wife or children?
o: Because wives and children have no legal standing in Temple matters
Because the source verse, 'if he be too poor for your valuation,' is read as an instruction to sustain specifically 'him,' not his wife and children
Because wives and children are always independently wealthy
Because this rule applies only to unmarried debtors
quiz.e: The Gemara reads Leviticus 27:8's 'he' as teaching that the treasurer sustains the debtor himself from his valuation debt — his wife and children are not included in that verse.

quiz.q: What did Rav Yeimar's ruling about a man who sold all his property come to teach, given that the mishna already states that one who consecrates his property has his tefillin taken?
o: That the mishna's ruling was mistaken
That even in an ordinary sale (not consecration) of 'everything,' tefillin are included too, despite the concern that people don't casually sell items used for a bodily mitzva without saying so
That tefillin can never be sold under any circumstances
That the buyer must return the tefillin voluntarily
quiz.e: The novel teaching is that even a plain sale of 'all his property' includes tefillin, even though one might have thought a person wouldn't silently include a mitzva item like tefillin in a sale unless he consecrated it (with clear mitzva-intent).

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, why doesn't the Temple treasury collect based on an item's potential future or appreciated value (like a fine garment increasing a slave's sale price, or a pearl sold in the city)?
o: Because such items cannot be sold to the Temple at all
Because the verse 'give your valuation on that day' teaches that value is fixed to its current location and time, not a later, higher price
Because the Temple treasury only accepts cash, never goods
Because appreciated value is always given to the poor instead
quiz.e: The baraita derives from 'and he shall give your valuation as of that day' (Lev. 27:23) that the Temple must value and collect an item based on its present location and moment, not by waiting for it to fetch a higher price.

quiz.q: According to Rav and Shmuel's joint statement, what does the mishna's rule 'one may not consecrate an ancestral field less than two years before the Jubilee' actually restrict?
o: It bans consecrating the field entirely during that window
It bans only redeeming the field with a year-prorated deduction during that window — consecration itself remains valid, just redeemed at full price
It applies only to fields owned by priests
It has no practical effect at all
quiz.e: Rav and Shmuel explain the mishna is about redemption 'with a deduction' (a discount based on years remaining) — consecration is still effective within two years of the Jubilee, but redemption must then be at the full fifty-sela valuation.

quiz.q: What is the core dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding a field consecrated DURING the Jubilee Year itself?
o: Rav says it is not consecrated at all; Shmuel says it is consecrated at full price
Rav says it is consecrated and redeemed for the full fifty sela; Shmuel says it is not consecrated at all, reading 'from the Jubilee Year' as excluding that year
Both agree it is not consecrated
Both agree it is consecrated but only redeemable with a deduction
quiz.e: Rav holds the verse 'if he sanctifies his field from the Jubilee Year' includes the Jubilee Year itself, so consecration is valid at full price; Shmuel reads 'from the Jubilee Year' as beginning only the following year, so consecration during the Jubilee Year itself has no effect.
